results.title: Closed topological 4-manifold
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A closed topological 4-manifold is a nonempty, compact, connected, Hausdorff, second-countable topological space $M$ together with an atlas of charts covering $M$, each a homeomorphism from an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^4$ (charts are modelled on all of $\mathbb{R}^4$, not on a half-space, so $M$ has no boundary).

results.title: Integral singular homology as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $k$ and a topological space $X$, $H_k(X; \mathbb{Z})$ is the $k$-th singular homology of $X$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$, viewed as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module.

results.title: Aspherical closed 4-manifold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A closed topological 4-manifold $M$ is aspherical if for every $k \ge 2$ and every point $x \in M$ the homotopy group $\pi_k(M, x)$ is trivial.

results.title: Integer homology 4-sphere
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A closed topological 4-manifold $M$ is an integer homology 4-sphere if for every $k \ge 0$ the integral singular homology $H_k(M; \mathbb{Z})$ is isomorphic, as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, to $H_k(S^4; \mathbb{Z})$, where $S^4$ is the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^5$.

results.title: Existence of an aspherical integer homology 4-sphere
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a closed connected topological 4-manifold $M$ that is aspherical, meaning that for every $k \ge 2$ and every point $x \in M$ the homotopy group $\pi_k(M, x)$ is trivial, and that is an integer homology 4-sphere, meaning that for every $k \ge 0$ the integral singular homology $H_k(M; \mathbb{Z})$ is isomorphic to $H_k(S^4; \mathbb{Z})$, where $S^4$ is the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^5$.

results.title: Quotient seminorm equals distance to the subspace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, and give $E/S$ the quotient seminorm. Then for every $x \in E$ the class $q(x)$ of $x$ under the quotient map $q \colon E \to E/S$ satisfies $\|q(x)\| = d(x, S)$, where $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

results.title: The quotient map has norm at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, and give $E/S$ the quotient seminorm. Then the quotient map $q \colon E \to E/S$, a continuous linear map, has operator norm $\|q\| \le 1$.

results.title: Hahn–Banach distance formula, attainment form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, not necessarily closed, and let $x \in E$. Then there is a continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| \le 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies $f(x) = d(x, S)$, where $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

results.title: Norm-one annihilating functional at positive distance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, and let $x \in E$ have positive distance $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\| > 0$ from $S$. Then there is a continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| = 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies $f(x) = d(x, S)$.

results.title: Norm-one annihilating functional outside a closed subspace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a closed linear subspace of $E$ and let $x \in E$ with $x \notin S$. Then there is a continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| = 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies $f(x) = d(x, S)$, where $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

results.title: Hahn–Banach distance formula
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, not necessarily closed, and let $x \in E$. Then the distance $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ from $x$ to $S$ equals the supremum of $|f(x)|$ over all continuous linear functionals $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| \le 1$ that vanish on $S$.

results.summary: A sequence $s \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a Van der Laan sequence when, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the four consecutive terms $s(n), s(n + 1), s(n + 2), s(n + 3)$ form a Van der Laan window, that is, the largest of them equals the sum of the two smallest.

results.title: Van der Laan windows in increasing order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a \le b \le c \le d$ be natural numbers. Then $a, b, c, d$ form a Van der Laan window if and only if $d = a + b$.

results.title: Constant Van der Laan windows
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $k$, the window $k, k, k, k$ is a Van der Laan window if and only if $k = 0$.

results.title: Constant Van der Laan sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $k$, the constant sequence $s \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $s(n) = k$ for all $n$ is a Van der Laan sequence if and only if $k = 0$.

results.title: Number of set partitions of given type and genus
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $g$ and a multiset $\alpha$ of natural numbers, $C_{n,[\alpha]}^{(g)}$ is the number of increasing-cycle permutations $\tau$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ whose multiset of cycle lengths, fixed points counted as cycles of length $1$, is $\alpha$ and whose genus is $g$.

results.title: The identity is an increasing-cycle permutation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the identity permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is an increasing-cycle permutation.

results.title: The partition into singletons has genus zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the genus of the identity permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is $0$; the identity encodes the partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ into singletons.

results.title: The cyclic rotation is an increasing-cycle permutation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the cyclic permutation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod n$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is an increasing-cycle permutation.

results.title: The one-block partition has genus zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the genus of the cyclic permutation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod n$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is $0$.

results.title: Multiway cut instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A multiway cut instance is a tuple $(n, E, T, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges), a list $T$ of natural numbers (the terminals) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of cut edges).

results.title: Well-formed multiway cut instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A multiway cut instance $(n, E, T, K)$ is well-formed when the entries of $E$ are pairwise distinct; every entry $(u, v)$ of $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ is not an entry of $E$; the entries of $T$ are pairwise distinct; and every entry $t$ of $T$ satisfies $t < n$. Thus $E$ lists each edge of a simple undirected graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ exactly once, in one orientation,…

results.title: Feasible multiway cut instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $(n, E, T, K)$ be a multiway cut instance with terminal list $T = (t_0, \dots, t_{k-1})$. It is feasible when there is a labelling $f$ of the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ by labels in $\{0, \dots, \max(k, 1) - 1\}$ such that $f(t_j) = j$ for every $j < k$, and at most $K$ entries $(u, v)$ of $E$, counted with repetition, satisfy $f(u) \ne f(v)$. Here every number $v \ge n$ counts as a vertex with label $0$.

results.title: The MULTIWAY CUT decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: MULTIWAY CUT is the decision problem on bitstrings that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a multiway cut instance $(n, E, T, K)$ that is well-formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to a multiway cut instance are rejected.

results.title: MULTIWAY CUT is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let MULTIWAY CUT be the decision problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings decoding to a well-formed, feasible multiway cut instance: a simple undirected graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, a list of distinct terminal vertices and a bound $K$ such that deleting at most $K$ edges of the graph leaves no two terminals connected. Then MULTIWAY CUT is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to MULTIWAY CUT…

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A k-center instance $(D, K, B)$ is well formed when all rows of $D$ have the same length.

results.title: Feasible k-center instances

For $c < m$ and a natural number $f$, write $D_c(f)$ for the entry of $D_c$ at position $f$, counting from $0$, and set $D_c(f) = 0$ if $D_c$ has at most $f$ entries. The instance is feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ locations $f < n$ such that every client $c < m$ has…

results.title: Generalized nonmetric k-center as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a k-center instance that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

results.title: k-CENTER (GENERALIZED, NONMETRIC) is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem of generalized nonmetric k-center on bitstrings is NP-complete: it belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Joint configurations of a set of variables
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The joint values of the variables in `S`.

results.title: Rising factorial
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The rising factorial `a (a + 1) ⋯ (a + n - 1)`, equal to `Γ(a + n) / Γ(a)` for `a > 0`.

results.title: Count of cases matching a configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of cases in `D` that take the values `c` on the variables `S`.

results.title: Bayesian–Dirichlet family score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Bayesian–Dirichlet score of a family `F` with parent set `P ⊆ F` and hyperparameters `α` on the configurations of `F`.

results.title: Bayesian–Dirichlet network score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The BD score of the structure `Pa` with family hyperparameters `α`: the product of the family scores.

results.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet prediction factor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet prediction factor for the case `x` after the cases `D`: `∏_v (α_{v,c} + n_{v,c}) / (α_{v,j} + n_{v,j})`, with `c`, `j` the family and parent values of `x` and `n` the counts in `D`. This is a genuine conditional probability only when `Pa` is a DAG; for arbitrary parent maps (e.g. cycles or self-parents) the factors over all cases need not sum to one.

results.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product after prior cases
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product for the cases `D`, in order, after the cases `E`: each case contributes its `predictive` factor given all cases before it. A genuine probability of the data only when `Pa` is a DAG (see `predictive`).

results.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product of the data
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product for the cases of `D`, in order. A genuine probability of the data only when `Pa` is a DAG (see `predictive`).

results.title: Parent configuration counts sum over family configurations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The number of cases matching a parent configuration is the sum over the family configurations extending it (`N_j = ∑_k N_jk`).

results.title: The BD score is the sequential prediction product
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The BD score is the sequential prediction product of the data (hence it does not depend on the order of the cases). This is an identity for all real hyperparameters. Positivity of the hyperparameters only makes every predictive denominator positive; it does not make this product a probability. The product is a genuine probability of the data only when `Pa` is a DAG with no self-parents: for cyclic parent maps the…

results.title: BDe hyperparameters
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: BDe hyperparameters (Heckerman, Geiger and Chickering): `ess` times the weight `∑_{x ↦ c} p x` of the configuration `c` of `S`. When `∑ x, p x = 1`, `p` is a prior joint distribution and this is the prior probability of `c`.

results.title: BDe marginal likelihood of a variable set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The (unnormalized) marginal likelihood of the data restricted to the variables `S` under the BDe Dirichlet prior on the joint values of `S`. `p` is treated as generalized weights here: the total Dirichlet mass over configurations is `ess * ∑ x, p x`, so the omitted normalizing factor is `1 / rising (ess * ∑ x, p x) D.length`, the same for every `S`. When `p` is normalized (`∑ x, p x = 1`) this is…

results.title: BDe family score as a ratio of marginal likelihoods
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With BDe hyperparameters, a family score is a ratio of set marginal likelihoods.

results.title: BDe network score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The BDe score of the structure `Pa`.

results.title: Covered-edge reversal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `Pa'` is obtained from `Pa` by reversing a covered edge `x → y` (Chickering 1995): `x` is a parent of `y` and `y`'s other parents are exactly `x`'s parents (`Pa y = insert x (Pa x)`); after the reversal `y` has parents `Pa x` and `x` has parents `insert y (Pa x)`. Acyclicity is not required: the score identity holds for any parent-set maps (on a DAG, `x ∉ Pa x` and `y ∉ Pa x` hold automatically).

results.title: Covered-edge reversal preserves the BDe score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Covered-edge reversal preserves the BDe score (for a positive weight function `p` — a prior when `∑ x, p x = 1` — and positive equivalent sample size).

results.title: Covered-edge reversals preserve the BDe score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Structures connected by a sequence of covered-edge reversals have the same BDe score.

results.title: Acyclic network structure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The structure has no directed cycle.

results.title: Adjacent vertices in a network structure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `u` and `w` are adjacent (joined by an edge in either direction).

results.title: V-structure in a directed graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `u → w ← z` is a v-structure: two non-adjacent distinct parents of a common child.

results.title: Chickering's transformational characterization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Chickering's transformational characterization (1995): two acyclic structures with the same skeleton and the same v-structures (Markov equivalent by Verma and Pearl) are connected by a sequence of covered-edge reversals.

results.title: Array binary search membership test agrees with binary search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be an array with entries in a type $\alpha$, let $k \in \alpha$, let $\mathrm{lt}$ be any Boolean-valued comparison on $\alpha$, and let $\ell$ and $h$ be natural numbers. Lean core's Boolean binary search membership test for $k$ in $A$, with comparison $\mathrm{lt}$ and bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns true exactly when Lean core's array binary search with the same arguments returns some element.

results.title: Result of bounded binary search on a sorted array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type, with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$. Let $k$ and $a$ be elements of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural numbers. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns $a$ if and only if $a = k$ and there is an index $i < n$ with…

results.title: Bounded binary search on a sorted array fails exactly when the key is absent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type, with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$. Let $k$ be an element of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural numbers. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns no element if and only if there is no index $i < n$ with $\ell \le i \le h$ and…

results.title: Bounded binary search membership test on a sorted array is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type, with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$. Let $k$ be an element of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural numbers. Lean core's Boolean binary search membership test for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns true if and only if there is an index $i < n$ with…

results.title: Binary search on a sorted array finds exactly its members
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be an array with entries in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later one, and let $k$ and $a$ be elements of that type. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ over the whole of $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns $a$ if and only if $a = k$ and $k$ is an entry of $A$.

results.title: Binary search on a sorted array fails exactly on non-members
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be an array with entries in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later one, and let $k$ be an element of that type. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ over the whole of $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns no element if and only if $k$ is not an entry of $A$.

results.title: Binary search membership test on a sorted array is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be an array with entries in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later one, and let $k$ be an element of that type. Lean core's Boolean binary search membership test for $k$ over the whole of $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns true if and only if $k$ is an entry of $A$.

results.title: Lower-bound search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $k$, lower-bound search maintains a half-open interval $[l, h)$ of indices, starting from $[0, n)$. While $l < h$, it compares $a_m$ with $k$ at the midpoint $m = l + \lfloor (h - l)/2 \rfloor$, charging one unit for this comparison, and continues with $[m + 1, h)$ if $a_m < k$ and with $[l, m)$ otherwise. When $l = h$ it returns $l$.

results.title: Correctness of lower-bound search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. Then $\ell \le n$, $a_j < k$ for every $j < \ell$, and $k \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $\ell \le j < n$.

results.title: Comparison bound for lower-bound search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$ makes at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ element comparisons.

results.title: Binary search for the first occurrence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ runs lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, obtaining an index $\ell$. If $\ell < n$, it makes one further comparison, charged one unit, and returns $\ell$ when $a_\ell = k$ and no index otherwise; if $\ell \ge n$, it returns no index without further cost.

results.title: Binary search returns the first occurrence of the key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key and let $i$ be a natural number. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns the index $i$ if and only if $i < n$, $a_i = k$, and $a_j < k$ for every $j < i$.

results.title: Binary search reports absence exactly when the key is absent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, and let $k$ be a key. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns no index if and only if $a_i \ne k$ for every $i < n$.

results.title: Exact comparison count of binary search for the first occurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. The number of element comparisons made by binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ equals the number made by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, plus $1$ if $\ell < n$ and plus $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Comparison bound for binary search for the first occurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ makes at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil + 1$ element comparisons.

results.title: Wright–Fisher transition probability of the lineage count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: One-generation transition probability of the ancestral lineage count in a neutral Wright–Fisher population of `M` gene copies: `k` lineages pick their parents uniformly and independently among `M` copies, and `j` distinct parents occur with probability `stirlingSecond k j * M.descFactorial j / M ^ k`.

results.title: Wright–Fisher transition matrix of the lineage count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The one-generation transition matrix of the ancestral lineage count of a sample of at most `n` gene copies in a Wright–Fisher population of `M` copies; row `k`, column `j` is `wfLineageProb M k j`.

results.title: Generator of Kingman's block-counting process
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The rate matrix of Kingman's block-counting (pure-death) process on `{0, …, n}`: `k` lineages become `k - 1` at rate `k.choose 2`, time in units of `M = 2N` generations.

results.title: Tavaré's formula for the number of ancestral lineages
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Tavaré's closed form for the probability that `i` lineages of Kingman's coalescent have `j` ancestors `t` time units (`2N` generations each) earlier, for `1 ≤ j ≤ i`.

results.title: Scaled Wright–Fisher lineage matrix converges to Kingman's generator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The scaled one-generation increment `M • (wfLineageMatrix n M - 1)` converges entrywise to the block-counting generator: `k` lineages coalesce to `k - 1` with probability `(k.choose 2) / M + o(1/M)`, and to fewer with probability `O(1/M²)`.

results.title: Kingman's theorem for the lineage count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `t ≥ 0`, the `⌊t M⌋`-generation transition matrix of the Wright–Fisher ancestral lineage count converges, as the population size `M` tends to infinity, to the transition matrix `exp (t • G)` of the pure-death process with rates `k.choose 2`.

results.title: Right eigenvectors of Kingman's block-counting generator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Right eigenvectors of the block-counting generator, as columns: column `k` has entries `i_{(k)} / i^{(k)}` (falling over rising factorial) and eigenvalue `-(k.choose 2)`.

results.title: Left eigenvectors of Kingman's block-counting generator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Left eigenvectors of the block-counting generator, as rows: row `0` is the indicator of state `0`, and for `1 ≤ k` row `k` has entries `(2k-1) (-1)^{k-j} j^{(k-1)} / (j! (k-j)!)` for `j ≤ k` and `0` for `j > k`; the eigenvalue is `-(k.choose 2)`.

results.title: Eigenvalues of Kingman's block-counting generator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The eigenvalues of the block-counting generator, `-(k.choose 2)`.

results.title: Right eigenvector equation for the block-counting generator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The columns of `blockCountingRightEigen n` are right eigenvectors: `G V = V D`.

results.title: Left eigenvector equation for the block-counting generator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The rows of `blockCountingLeftEigen n` are left eigenvectors: `W G = D W`.

results.title: Left and right eigenvector matrices are mutually inverse
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The left and right eigenvector matrices are mutually inverse: `W V = 1`.

results.title: Spectral decomposition of the block-counting transition matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The spectral decomposition of the transition matrix of the block-counting process: `exp (t • G) = V diag(exp (-(k.choose 2) t)) W`.

results.title: Tavaré's formula
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The transition probabilities of Kingman's block-counting process from `i` to `j` lineages in time `t`, for `1 ≤ j ≤ i ≤ n`, are given by `tavareProb`.

results.title: Truncation consistency
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `n ≤ N`, the top-left `(n + 1) × (n + 1)` block of the transition matrix `exp (t • G)` of the block-counting process on `{0, …, N}` is the transition matrix of the process on `{0, …, n}` (the process only moves down). Holds for every real `t`.

results.title: The block-counting process never gains lineages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The block-counting process never gains lineages: `exp (t • G) i j = 0` for `i < j`. Holds for every real `t`.
